messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: warmup
parts:
Hi,

Is it possible to implement sampler so that warmup ends when some significant mixing is determined?  To alleviate the problem of infinite warmup perhaps some max warmup setting is needed.  Technically if mixing is not determined then sampling is not meaningful (this is just my inexperienced opinion).

Based on my simulations I found that often times mixing is reach much before than it was set what means that time was spent inefficiently.  Even when priors are changed from non-informative to slightly informative mixing may occur sooner than expected (and vice versa).  This enhancement could make sweep runs more efficient.

Linas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup (& convergence)
parts:
We've discussed this kind of thing at length before
and when we build in the functionality to allow restarting,
it should be much easier to experiment with. Then when we have
a method that works, we can implement it. We're all ears if
you have concrete suggestions.

Let me summarize the discussion so far.

The target of warmup is to

1. find the high volume mass of the posterior, i.e., get
our first effective sample, and

2. estimate the step size (time discretization) and mass
matrix (Euclidean metric).

We know we've done (1) and (2) well when we are sampling well in
terms of effective samples per iteration.

We have the chicken and egg problem of needing a good step size and
mass matrix (2) before we can effectively find the high volume mass
of the posterior (1), but we need to find the high volume mass of the
posterior (1) before we can effectively estimate step size (2).

The problem with evaluating our mixing-well criterion is that we don't
know what's optimal. The only way to evaluate that is to do more
adaptation and see if it changes anything.

So what we tend to do now is just be conservative in how long warmup
runs (half total run time), and to suggest continuing to double the
overall number of iterations until you have a high enough n_eff. At
most this is going to cause something like a 50% inefficiency versus
optimal tuning.

- Bob
